The document provides specifications for major pesticide application equipment used in vector control. These guidelines aim to assist national authorities and public health users in selecting high-quality equipment for pesticide application. The second edition includes specifications for equipment used for larvicides and some additional equipment for adulticides. The test methods described are intended to ensure that the equipment functions for at least three years with proper maintenance. Manufacturers are required to provide warranties against manufacturing defects, after-sales service, and compliance with national or international specifications. WHO no longer tests pesticide application equipment for compliance with its specifications. National programs or agencies wishing to evaluate specific equipment must arrange testing with a WHO-approved laboratory. Manufacturers can also arrange for their equipment to be tested at recognized laboratories. Feedback on equipment performance is welcomed to validate compliance with WHO specifications. Manufacturers must supply operating and maintenance manuals in relevant languages and provide technical support through authorized distributors. They should also assist in training local vector control staff in proper equipment use, maintenance, and storage practices. WHO specifications are designed to meet the specific requirements of vector control and, where possible, align with ISO standards for pesticide application equipment. The document outlines various pesticide application techniques used in vector control, including indoor residual spraying, space spraying, larval control, and barrier treatments. Indoor residual spraying involves applying insecticide to interior wall surfaces to control mosquitoes that rest indoors. This method is one of WHO's core malaria interventions and is being investigated for dengue control. Hand compression sprayers are commonly used for this purpose, and the equipment must include a pressure control valve to maintain consistent output. Space treatments require the production of extremely small droplets that remain airborne long enough to target flying insects. This method applies a low dose of insecticide with no residual effect, minimizing environmental impact and protecting pollinators. Space treatments are particularly important for controlling outdoor-active mosquitoes and involve equipment ranging from small aerosol cans to larger machines, including thermal and cold foggers.
